title: File:Jura-Gelb.jpg
description: Polished slab of a limestone of the Treuchtlingen Formation of the middle part of the Weißjura (Kimmeridgian) of the Franconian Alb (size ca 8×12 cm). In dimension stone business this limestone variety is called Jura-Marmor (“Jura marble”) or Treuchtlinger Marmor (“Treuchtlingen marble”). The white-speckled appearance is caused by the presence of the microfossil Tubiphytes morronensis (also Crescentiella morronensis) which is often assigned to the Foraminifera.

description: Pikes Peak Granite (pgpm2 facies) from a little east of the summit house of Pikes Peak. This facies is coarsely- to very coarsely-crystalline and porphyritic. description: View is to the southwest. These slabs are on display outside near the entrance. In the past, much larger slabs were quarried, cut & polished for use as flooring and window sills in abbeys, churches, cathedrals, friaries & monasteries primarily. Today, only small pieces of Connemara Marble are sold, as the supply is starting to dwindle.

title: File:Slabbed Septarian Nodule Discovery Near Holland, Michigan.jpg
description: Septarian Nodules are ancient, fossilized mineral formations that contain calcite, aragonite, and limestone. These nodules are often polished to reveal the intricate patterns inside, with striking lines of yellow, brown, and white. This piece (viewed through an eye loupe), found near Holland, Michigan, showcases the beauty of these natural treasures, which formed millions of years ago when sediment collected around decaying sea life, eventually becoming the nodules we see today.

title: File:Chondrodite marble (GeoDIL number - 245).jpg
description: Most of this sample is white calcite, CaCO3. The light brown to gray mineral is chondrodite, (Mg,Fe)5(SiO4)2(F,OH)2, but chondrodite usually has a more yellowish color. Chondrodite belongs to the humite group, and is closely related to olivine. Also present are graphite and a white mica, but they can only be seen in the highest resolution photo. This sample measures approximately 10 cm across.

title: File:Pink marble (GeoDIL number - 324).jpg
description: This sample of the Murphy Marble is nearly entirely made of calcite. Minor phlogopite, apatite and rutile can be seen in thin section. This specimen is 9 cm across.

title: File:Franklin Marble (dolomite marble) (GeoDIL number - 325).jpg
description: This sample of the Franklin Marble is composed mainly of dolomite. The few dark mineral grains are graphite and phlogopite. This specimen is 10 cm across.

title: File:Graphitic marble (GeoDIL number - 504).jpg
description: This marble is dark gray because of the presence of graphite. Also present, but not visible in hand specimen, is phlogopite (a mica). This sample is 9.5 cm across.

title: File:Lee Marble (dolomitic) (GeoDIL number - 505).jpg
description: Typical limestones are dominated by calcite, but many contain dolomite. Some are nearly 100% dolomite. When limestones are metamorphosed to produce marble, the dominant carbonate does not change. This marble, mostly dolomite, was first mined in the 1850s. The Lee marble is an exceptionally tough marble and has been used as building stone in many places, including the base of the Washington Monument. It is also a common marble used for gravestones, especially at Arlington National Cemetary and ot

title: File:Marble (GeoDIL number - 506).jpg
description: This 10 cm wide marble sample is from the Adirondack lowlands in upstate New York. It is nearly 100% calcite, but close examination reveals a few brown flakes of phlogopite and some silvery specks of graphite. Some marbles contain conspicuous metamorphic minerals. This one does not because it formed from metamorphism of a limestone that contained little but calcite, so the chemical components needed to form new metamorphic minerals were not present.

title: File:White marble (GeoDIL number - 507).jpg
description: Marble forms by metamorphism of limestone. This marble was a commonly used building stone in the 19th and early 20th century. It was first quarried around 1807. Later, it was mined from underground. Activity peaked in the mid to late 1800s but declined in the 20th century. Most mines closed between 1930 and 1950. Today, most of the quarries and mines are filled with water. This sample is about 9 cm by 6 cm. It is nearly 100% calcite.

title: File:Brown marble (GeoDIL number - 508).jpg
description: Marbles (metamorphosed limestones or dolostones) are typically white, but just about any color is possible. Microscope examination of this sample reveals that it was a biogenic limestone prior to metamorphism. The brown color, at least in part, appears due to organic matter that survived metamorphism. Some hematite is also present and adds some red to the color. This sample is 8 cm wide.

title: File:White marble (GeoDIL number - 509).jpg
description: Marbles are metamorphosed limestones or dolostones. They are highly variable in color and character, but classic marble is white and polishes to produce smooth resistant surfaces. This high-quality marble is 99% calcite with very minor phlogopite present as small light brown-yellow flakes. It is quarried by the Georgia Marble Company in Tate, Georgia. Tate marble is used around the world as building, monument and grave stone. This sample is 8.5 cm across.

title: File:Marble (GeoDIL number - 510).jpg
description: This sample from Lucerne Valley, California, USA, contains both calcite and dolomite. The calcite is grayish with a very light blue tinge; the dolomite is lighter - almost white. The two minerals are very difficult to distinguish in hand specimen and in thin section without using a chemical stain. Ward’s Scientific calls this a “blue-gray” marble, but it takes an active imagination to see the blue. Some marbles, including the classic marble from Crestmore, California (not far from Lucerne Valley

title: File:Travertine (GeoDIL number - 697).jpg
description: Travertine forms at hot springs when warm waters rich in calcium carbonate bubble up and cool, precipitating calcite. Although travertine is always a form of calcite, it generally appears banded because different layers grow under different conditions and may have slightly different chemistries. Travertine is often used as an ornamental or building stone but is quite soft.

title: File:Marble (cipolino) (GeoDIL number - 722).jpg
description: This is a polished slab of a type of marble called Cipolino. It is mostly calcite with darker layers containing blue-gray quartz. Marble is a general name given to metamorphosed limestones and dolostones; marbles may have any of many different appearances. Marble is relatively soft and easy to cut and shape, and so is often used as building stone or in art works. This slab is 11 cm across.

title: File:Marble containing phlogopite and chondrodite (GeoDIL number - 724).jpg
description: Marble is a general name for rocks formed by metamorphism of a limestone or dolostone. Marbles are dominated by calcite or dolomite, but some contain any of a number of interesting accessory minerals. This sample contains very light brown flakes of phlogopite (Mg-rich biotite) and darker brown granular grains of chondrodite (an Mg-Fe mineral related to olivine).

title: File:Kossuthplatz, Millennium-Denkmal, Tafel, 2026 Tiszafüred.jpg
description: Millennium Monument, a work by Béla Gerenday, sculptor (Unveiled on September 12, 1896). The twelve-meter-tall obelisk, carved from Sóskút limestone. Polished Carrara marble plaques were affixed to all four sides of the column. On the marble slab on one side of the column is inscribed a classical, metrical poem written for this occasion by Ádám Lipcsey (1864–1910), a native of Tiszafüred - Kossuth Square, Tiszafüred, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County, Hungary.
